newsitem.title: USA: Officials try to gauge Dakota livestock losses.
newsitem.headline: Officials try to gauge Dakota livestock losses.

text.p: Cattle producers in the Dakotas will lose animals because of severe winter weather, but officials said Tuesday that the degree of damage may not be known for another few days or even weeks.
State and federal officials held a conference call meeting Tuesday to try to assess the extent of livestock casualties.

Dale Greenwood, president of the North Dakota's Stockmen's Association, participated in the call. He told Reuters that he estimated as much as five percent of the herd in western North Dakota could be wiped out by the weather.
Greenwood also said representatives from Indian reservations in North Dakota reported during the conference call that they could lose much as 15 percent of their herd.

Wayne Carlson, director of livestock for the North Dakota Department of Agriculture, said officials were working to estimate how many cattle had died as a result of the severe winter weather. But Carlson said the estimate would probably not be made available for another two weeks.
Cattle consume more feed in order to keep warm during cold weather. But North Dakota producers have faced a variety of obstacles this winter in supplying enough feed to their herds.
For starters, heavy autumn rains and an early snowstorm kept producers from retrieving hay that they had intended to use as feed throughout the winter.
"A lot of the feed is out in the fields buried in snow, and (producers') equipment just is not big enough to go out and get it," Carlson said.
Recent blizzards and ensuing snow drifts have compounded the situation, paralyzing efforts to transport grain and thereby preventing producers from replenishing their feed supplies.

Larry Lampl, agriculture programs specialist for the North Dakota Farm Service Agency (FSA), estimated that 10,000 animals across the state were in dire need of feed. South Dakota's FSA estimated 16,000 animals were in that same predicament.
"They are in a position where they need to have feed immediately or there could be some losses," Lampl said.

Lampl said the problem appeared more severe in southwest regions of North Dakota and in north central South Dakota, where more producers tend to graze their cattle on pasture instead of keeping them in feedyards during the winter.
Producers in Sioux County, in south central North Dakota, were in the process of reporting losses to county authorities.

"The last report I had was that anywhere between 150 and 200 head (had died in Sioux County alone) and that's going to mount quickly," Sioux County Commissioner Rodney Froelich told Reuters. "My estimate would be closer to 300 head. People have a really tough time getting to their feed supplies because the snow up here is like cement."
Randy Blach, director of market analysis for CattleFax, a private cattle research firm in Colorado, said it was still too early to gauge the degree of livestock casualties.
"There's obviously been some losses. We're still in the process of pulling that together and the weather continues to be pretty bad through the northern tier of states," Blach said.
